claims.claim: vGAT exocytosis proceeded unperturbed under perturbation of actin dynamics.
claims.source: vGAT exocytosis proceeded unperturbed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: A dynamic actin cytoskeleton facilitates presynaptic endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Hence, a dynamic actin cytoskeleton facilitates presynaptic endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that perturbation of actin dynamics delays endocytosis.

claims.claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of Diaph1, encoding mDia1 (shmDia1), from hippocampal neurons led to significantly delayed Syph-pHluorin endocytosis and re-acidification in response to stimulation with 200 APs.
claims.source: We confirmed that shRNA-mediated depletion of Diaph1, encoding mDia1 (shmDia1), from hippocampal neurons led to significantly delayed Syph-pHluorin endocytosis and re-acidification in response to stimulation with 200 APs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Re-expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type mDia1 fully restored normal endocytosis kinetics in mDia1-depleted neurons.
claims.source: Re-expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type mDia1 fully restored normal endocytosis kinetics (Figure 1E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: Impaired SV endocytosis in lentivirus-mediated mDia1-depleted neurons was observed if SV exo-/endocytosis was triggered by stimulation with 40 APs or 80 APs and probed with vGLUT1-pHluorin.
claims.source: Impaired SV endocytosis in lentivirus-mediated mDia1-depleted neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) was also observed, if SV exo-/endocytosis was triggered by stimulation with 40 APs or 80 APs and probed with vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (vGLUT1)-pHluorin (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: Exocytic fusion of vGLUT1-pHluorin-containing SVs was unaffected by mDia1 depletion.
claims.source: Exocytic fusion of vGLUT1-pHluorin-containing SVs was unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Co-depletion of the closely related mDia3 isoform tended to further aggravate the endocytic phenotype caused by mDia1 loss.
claims.source: Co-depletion of the closely related mDia3 isoform tended to further aggravate this phenotype (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and K) without impacting the apparent number of fused SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and L) or vGAT exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: mDia1/3 depletion did not impact the apparent number of fused SVs.
claims.source: Co-depletion of the closely related mDia3 isoform tended to further aggravate this phenotype (Figure 1G and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and K) without impacting the apparent number of fused SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and L) or vGAT exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and L.

claims.claim: mDia1/3 depletion significantly delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT.
claims.source: Furthermore, mDia1/3 depletion significantly delayed the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT (Figure 1I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claims.claim: Application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins, led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin.
claims.source: Conversely, the application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that acts by relieving autoinhibition (Lash et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 1K and L) but no change in apparent SV fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K and L, and by citation to Lash et al., 2013.

claims.claim: IMM-01 acts by relieving autoinhibition of mDia-related formins.
claims.source: Conversely, the application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that acts by relieving autoinhibition (Lash et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 1K and L) but no change in apparent SV fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lash et al., 2013 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claims.claim: IMM-01 application caused no change in apparent SV fusion.
claims.source: Conversely, the application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that acts by relieving autoinhibition (Lash et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), led to a moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 1K and L) but no change in apparent SV fusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claims.claim: Ultrastructural analysis of hippocampal synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons by electron microscopy revealed a reduction in SV density compared to controls.
claims.source: Ultrastructural analysis of hippocampal synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons by electron microscopy revealed a reduction in SV density compared to controls (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: The reduction in SV density in mDia1/3-depleted neurons was rescued upon prior silencing of endogenous neuronal network activity in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
claims.source: This phenotype was rescued upon prior silencing of endogenous neuronal network activity in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: A similar, slightly more pronounced depletion of SVs was observed in hippocampal synapses from Diaph1 knockout (mDia1KO) mice.
claims.source: A similar, slightly more pronounced depletion of SVs was observed in hippocampal synapses from Diaph1 knockout (mDia1KO) mice (Peng et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2003; Shinohara et al., 2012; Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E, and by citations to Peng et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2003; Shinohara et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Mutant mDia1 lacking its N-terminal membrane-binding region (mDia1-ΔN) displayed reduced association with membranes in transfected HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Mutant mDia1-ΔN displayed reduced association with membranes in transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) and was unable to restore normal kinetics of Syph-pHluorin endocytosis in hippocampal neurons transfected with Diaph1-specific microRNA (shmDia1miR; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Mutant mDia1-ΔN was unable to restore normal kinetics of Syph-pHluorin endocytosis in hippocampal neurons transfected with Diaph1-specific microRNA.
claims.source: Mutant mDia1-ΔN displayed reduced association with membranes in transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) and was unable to restore normal kinetics of Syph-pHluorin endocytosis in hippocampal neurons transfected with Diaph1-specific microRNA (shmDia1miR; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: mDia may act on SV endocytosis by specifically promoting actin assembly at presynaptic membranes.
claims.source: Hence, mDia may act on SV endocytosis by specifically promoting actin assembly at presynaptic membranes.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that membrane-binding is required for mDia1 function in endocytosis.

claims.claim: Endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, where it is concentrated at or very close to the plasma membrane.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, where it is concentrated at or very close to the plasma membrane (Figure 3C and D), i.e., <50 nm away from the presynaptic membrane see Dani et al., 2010.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multicolor time-gated STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and D, and by citation to Dani et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Endogenous mDia1 is <50 nm away from the presynaptic membrane.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, where it is concentrated at or very close to the plasma membrane (Figure 3C and D), i.e., <50 nm away from the presynaptic membrane see Dani et al., 2010.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data and citation to Dani et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Quantitative proteomic analyses of mDia1 immunoprecipitates from detergent-extracted mouse synaptosomes identified actin, Myosin IIB, and the small GTPase Rac1 as interaction partners.
claims.source: Prompted by these results we dissected the interactome of mDia1 by unbiased quantitative proteomic analyses of immunoprecipiates from detergent-extracted mouse synaptosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). In addition to actin, we identified a variety of additional actin-regulatory proteins including Myosin IIB (Chandrasekar et al., 2013) and the small GTPase Rac1 (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and by citation to Chandrasekar et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The association of mDia1 with actin and Myosin IIB was confirmed by immunoprecipitation.
claims.source: We confirmed the association of mDia1 with actin and Myosin IIB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and found Myosin IIB to be concentrated at or near the presynaptic plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G) akin to the localization of mDia1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Myosin IIB is concentrated at or near the presynaptic plasma membrane akin to the localization of mDia1.
claims.source: We confirmed the association of mDia1 with actin and Myosin IIB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and found Myosin IIB to be concentrated at or near the presynaptic plasma membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G) akin to the localization of mDia1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claims.claim: The association of mDia1 with Myosin IIB is consistent with the inhibitory effects of the Myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin on SV endocytosis.
claims.source: The association of mDia1 with Myosin IIB is consistent with the inhibitory effects of the Myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin on SV endocytosis (Chandrasekar et al., 2013; Soykan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chandrasekar et al., 2013 and Soykan et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Several endocytic proteins previously implicated in SV recycling were enriched in mDia1 immunoprecipitates, including Synaptojanin1, Amphiphysin, Endophilin A1, PACSIN1/2, and Dynamin1.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also observed an enrichment of several endocytic proteins previously implicated in SV recycling in mDia1 immunoprecipitates. These include the lipid phosphatase Synaptojanin1, the bin-amphiphysin-rvs (BAR) domain proteins Amphiphysin, Endophilin A1, and PACSIN1/2 and, the GTPase Dynamin1 (Chanaday et al., 2019; Gan and Watanabe, 2018; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012; Soykan et al., 2016; Figure 3E) as confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3E and immunoblotting data in Figure 3F, and by citations to Chanaday et al., 2019; Gan and Watanabe, 2018; Saheki and De Camilli, 2012; Soykan et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Application of the partially non-selective Dynamin inhibitor Dynasore led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
claims.source: Application of the partially non-selective Dynamin inhibitor Dynasore (Macia et al., 2006; Figure 3C and H) or expression of dominant-negative mutant Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 3G1) led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and H, and by citation to Macia et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Expression of dominant-negative mutant Dynamin1 K44A led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
claims.source: Application of the partially non-selective Dynamin inhibitor Dynasore (Macia et al., 2006; Figure 3C and H) or expression of dominant-negative mutant Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 3G1) led to a significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites marked by Bassoon.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: mDia1 levels at the postsynapse were increased following Dynasore treatment or expression of dominant-negative Dynamin1.
claims.source: mDia1 levels at the postsynapse were also increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: Dynasore did not impact the levels or distribution of Bassoon or Homer1.
claims.source: Dynasore did not impact the levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J) or distribution of Bassoon or Homer1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claims.claim: Endogenous presynaptic F-actin labeled by phalloidin was highly abundant at the postsynaptic compartment and also visible, albeit at reduced levels, in presynaptic boutons marked by Bassoon.
claims.source: Multicolor gSTED imaging confirmed that F-actin labeled by phalloidin was highly abundant at the postsynaptic compartment. In addition, F-actin was also visible, albeit at reduced levels, in presynaptic boutons marked by Bassoon (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Dynamin in the presence of Dynasore significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
claims.source: Inhibition of Dynamin in the presence of Dynasore (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or expression of Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Expression of Dynamin1 K44A significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
claims.source: Inhibition of Dynamin in the presence of Dynasore (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or expression of Dynamin1 K44A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) significantly elevated presynaptic F-actin levels within the Bassoon area.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: Actin polymerization-defective mutant mDia1 (K994A) failed to restore delayed vGLUT1-pHluorin endocytosis in mDia1-depleted hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: We found that actin polymerization-defective mutant mDia1 (K994A) failed to restore delayed vGLUT1-pHluorin endocytosis in mDia1-depleted hippocampal neurons (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced the amount of detectable F-actin within the Bassoon area.
claims.source: We found that loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced the amount of detectable F-actin within the Bassoon area (Figure 4A and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and E.

claims.claim: Loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced endogenous β-actin at presynapses in eGFP-Actb knock-in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: This assay confirmed the significant reduction in endogenous β-actin at presynapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons (Figure 4F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and G using genome-engineered neurons.

claims.claim: Treatment of mDia1/3-depleted neurons with jasplakinolide fully restored the kinetics of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin.
claims.source: Treatment of mDia1/3-depleted neurons with jasplakinolide indeed fully restored the kinetics of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and rescued presynaptic F-actin levels to that of controls (actin levels normalized to shCTR + DMSO, set to 100: shCTR + DMSO = 100 ± 6.3; shmDia1+3 + DMSO=47.7 ± 4.3; shCTR + Jasp = 150.6 ± 11.9; shmDia1+3 + Jasp=94.3 ± 11.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: Jasplakinolide treatment rescued presynaptic F-actin levels in mDia1/3-depleted neurons to that of controls.
claims.source: Treatment of mDia1/3-depleted neurons with jasplakinolide indeed fully restored the kinetics of SV endocytosis monitored by vGLUT1-pHluorin (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and rescued presynaptic F-actin levels to that of controls (actin levels normalized to shCTR + DMSO, set to 100: shCTR + DMSO = 100 ± 6.3; shmDia1+3 + DMSO=47.7 ± 4.3; shCTR + Jasp = 150.6 ± 11.9; shmDia1+3 + Jasp=94.3 ± 11.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: mDia1/3 facilitates SV endocytosis by regulating presynaptic F-actin.
claims.source: We conclude that mDia1/3 facilitates SV endocytosis by regulating presynaptic F-actin.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing the relationship between mDia1/3, F-actin, and endocytosis.

claims.claim: Endogenous RhoA was mostly located within the presynaptic compartment.
claims.source: Multicolor gSTED imaging revealed that endogenous RhoA was mostly located within the presynaptic compartment (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: Interference with Rho function by co-expression of dominant-negative variants of RhoA and RhoB delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis.
claims.source: Interference with Rho function by co-expression of dominant-negative (DN) variants of RhoA and RhoB (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or co-depletion of these Rho isoforms, by shRNA-mediated targeting of Rhoa and Rhob genes (shRhoA +B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B, and D.

claims.claim: Co-depletion of RhoA and RhoB by shRNA-mediated targeting delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis.
claims.source: Interference with Rho function by co-expression of dominant-negative (DN) variants of RhoA and RhoB (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or co-depletion of these Rho isoforms, by shRNA-mediated targeting of Rhoa and Rhob genes (shRhoA +B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), delayed SV endocytosis in response to stimulation with 200 APs without impacting the apparent levels of exocytosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, B, and D.

claims.claim: RhoA activity was reduced in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3.
claims.source: Consistently, we found that RhoA activity was reduced in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3 (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RhoA-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Rac1 activity was significantly elevated in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3.
claims.source: In agreement with the alleged antagonistic regulation of RhoA and Rac1 function (Lawson and Ridley, 2018), we found Rac1 activity to be significantly elevated in hippocampal neurons depleted of mDia1/3 (Figure 6B and C), e.g., under conditions of reduced Rho-GTP levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Rac1-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 6B and C, and by citation to Lawson and Ridley, 2018.

claims.claim: A similar increase in active Rac1 levels was observed upon pharmacological inhibition of RhoA/B in the presence of Rhosin.
claims.source: A similar increase in active Rac1 levels was observed upon pharmacological inhibition of RhoA/B in the presence of Rhosin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Rac1-GTP pulldown assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Rac1 was equally distributed between pre- and postsynaptic compartments in unperturbed hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Multicolor gSTED imaging showed that Rac1 was equally distributed between pre- and postsynaptic compartments in unperturbed hippocampal neurons (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: Selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C) and caused a delay in the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT (Figure 6F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: Selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 caused a delay in the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT.
claims.source: In support of this hypothesis, we found that selective pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C) and caused a delay in the endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT (Figure 6F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claims.claim: Rac1 inhibition appeared to further aggravate impaired vGAT endocytosis in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, although the effect remained below statistical significance.
claims.source: Moreover, Rac1 inhibition appeared to further aggravate impaired vGAT endocytosis in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, although the effect remained below statistical significance.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations that did not reach statistical significance.

claims.claim: Expression of constitutively active GTP-locked Rac1 (Rac1-CA) restored normal Syph-pHluorin endocytosis kinetics in mDia1/3-depleted neurons.
claims.source: Expression of constitutively active GTP-locked Rac1 (Rac1-CA) restored normal Syph-pHluorin endocytosis kinetics in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, whereas Syph-pHluorin endocytosis was delayed upon expression of dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) and exacerbated the endocytic phenotype of mDia1/3 loss (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Syph-pHluorin endocytosis was delayed upon expression of dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) and exacerbated the endocytic phenotype of mDia1/3 loss.
claims.source: Expression of constitutively active GTP-locked Rac1 (Rac1-CA) restored normal Syph-pHluorin endocytosis kinetics in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, whereas Syph-pHluorin endocytosis was delayed upon expression of dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) and exacerbated the endocytic phenotype of mDia1/3 loss (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: No overt effect of Rac1 inhibition or overexpression of either Rac1 form on SV exocytosis was observed.
claims.source: No overt effect of Rac1 inhibition or overexpression of either Rac1 form on SV exocytosis was observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and F.

claims.claim: Perturbation of Cdc42 did not significantly affect the kinetics of SV endocytosis in control or mDia1/3-depleted neurons.
claims.source: Perturbation of the related Cdc42 protein, another actin regulatory GTPase Lawson and Ridley, 2018 found at synapses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–I), did not significantly affect the kinetics of SV endocytosis in control or mDia1/3-depleted neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J and K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J and K, and by citation to Lawson and Ridley, 2018.

claims.claim: Synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons displayed an accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations that were found both in the vicinity of the active zone as well as distal from the synaptic contact area.
claims.source: Synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons displayed an accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations that were found both in the vicinity of the active zone as well as distal from the synaptic contact area (Figure 7A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claims.claim: Synapses from mDia1/3-depleted neurons displayed elevated numbers of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs).
claims.source: Moreover, we observed elevated numbers of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs) (Figure 7A and C) that might serve as a donor membrane for SV reformation (Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Kononenko et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2014) as suggested by the observed reduction in SV numbers in mDia-depleted neurons (compare Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and C, and by citations to Kononenko and Haucke, 2015; Kononenko et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2014.

claims.claim: A prominent accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations was found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
claims.source: A prominent accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and endosome-like vacuoles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) was similarly found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: A prominent accumulation of endosome-like vacuoles was found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
claims.source: A prominent accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and endosome-like vacuoles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) was similarly found in hippocampal neurons from mDia1 KO mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 led to the accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations.
claims.source: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 also led to the accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7A and D), whereas the number of endosome-like vacuoles was not significantly altered (Figure 7A and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and D.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 did not significantly alter the number of endosome-like vacuoles.
claims.source: Inhibition of Rac1 function by EHT 1864 also led to the accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 7A and D), whereas the number of endosome-like vacuoles was not significantly altered (Figure 7A and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and E.

claims.claim: Pharmacological blockade of Rac1 activity in neurons depleted of mDia1/3 further increased the number of plasma membrane invaginations significantly.
claims.source: Pharmacological blockade of Rac1 activity in neurons depleted of mDia1/3 further increased the number of plasma membrane invaginations significantly, while the additional effect on the number of endosome-like vacuoles remained insignificant (Figure 7F, G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F, G and H.

claims.claim: The additional effect of Rac1 blockade on the number of endosome-like vacuoles in mDia1/3-depleted neurons remained insignificant.
claims.source: Pharmacological blockade of Rac1 activity in neurons depleted of mDia1/3 further increased the number of plasma membrane invaginations significantly, while the additional effect on the number of endosome-like vacuoles remained insignificant (Figure 7F, G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F, G and H.

claims.claim: mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 perturbation exhibited similar phenotypes with respect to the length and width of tubular membrane invaginations.
claims.source: mDia1/3 loss and Rac1 perturbation exhibited similar phenotypes with respect to the length and width of tubular membrane invaginations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).

results.result: Pharmacological perturbation of actin dynamics using a cocktail of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 significantly delays synaptic vesicle endocytosis without affecting exocytosis in hippocampal neurons. This demonstrates that a dynamic actin cytoskeleton facilitates presynaptic endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide converging evidence from both exogenous (Syph-pHluorin) and endogenous (vGAT) markers showing delayed endocytosis with preserved exocytosis upon actin perturbation. The use of multiple drug combinations (C3-C4) and controls strengthens the conclusion that dynamic actin is required for endocytosis.

results.result: Genetic depletion of mDia1 alone or in combination with mDia3 significantly delays synaptic vesicle endocytosis without affecting exocytosis. This phenotype is rescued by re-expression of wild-type mDia1, demonstrating specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 demonstrate consistent endocytic delays across multiple stimulation protocols (40, 80, 200 APs) and markers (Syph-pHluorin, vGLUT1-pHluorin, vGAT-CypHer). The rescue experiment (C10) provides critical specificity control, and the lack of exocytic defects (C12, C14) indicates selective endocytic impairment.

results.result: Pharmacological activation of mDia formins using IMM-01 moderately accelerates synaptic vesicle endocytosis without affecting exocytosis, providing gain-of-function evidence for mDia's role in endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 provide complementary gain-of-function data supporting the loss-of-function experiments. The moderate acceleration (C16) is consistent with the drug's mechanism (C17), and the lack of exocytic effects (C18) parallels the loss-of-function phenotype.

results.result: mDia1/3 depletion causes a reduction in synaptic vesicle density that is activity-dependent, as demonstrated by rescue with tetrodotoxin treatment and similar phenotypes in mDia1 knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 provide ultrastructural evidence for the functional consequences of mDia loss. The TTX rescue (C20) demonstrates activity-dependence, and the consistency with genetic knockout mice (C21) validates the knockdown approach.

results.result: The N-terminal membrane-binding region of mDia1 is required for its function in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, suggesting that mDia acts by promoting actin assembly specifically at presynaptic membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 demonstrate that membrane localization is necessary for mDia1 function through structure-function analysis. The failure of the ΔN mutant to rescue endocytosis despite retaining actin-nucleating activity supports the inference (C24) that membrane-localized actin assembly is critical.

results.result: Endogenous mDia1 is localized to the presynaptic compartment within 50 nm of the plasma membrane, as determined by super-resolution STED microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 provide nanoscale localization data using STED microscopy with appropriate spatial resolution. The <50 nm distance measurement is consistent with the cited methodology (Dani et al., 2010) and supports membrane-proximal localization.

results.result: Proteomic analysis reveals that mDia1 associates with actin-regulatory proteins (Myosin IIB, Rac1) and endocytic machinery (Synaptojanin1, Amphiphysin, Endophilin A1, PACSIN1/2, Dynamin1) at synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 provide comprehensive proteomic and validation data identifying mDia1 interaction partners. The immunoprecipitation confirmations (C28) and STED localization of Myosin IIB (C29) strengthen the proteomic findings. The consistency with known endocytic functions (C30-C31) supports biological relevance.

results.result: Inhibition of dynamin-dependent endocytosis causes accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites without affecting synaptic markers, suggesting mDia1 accumulates at stalled endocytic intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 demonstrate mDia1 accumulation using both pharmacological (Dynasore) and genetic (K44A) approaches. The lack of effects on Bassoon/Homer1 (C35) indicates specificity, and the postsynaptic accumulation (C34) suggests broader membrane trafficking involvement.

results.result: Presynaptic F-actin is detectable at lower levels than postsynaptic F-actin and accumulates at presynaptic sites when dynamin-dependent endocytosis is blocked.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 establish baseline F-actin distribution and demonstrate accumulation upon endocytic blockade using both pharmacological and genetic approaches. This provides evidence linking F-actin to endocytic intermediates.

results.result: mDia1's actin polymerization activity is required for its function in endocytosis, and loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduces presynaptic F-actin levels as measured by phalloidin staining and endogenous β-actin imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 provide critical mechanistic evidence linking mDia1's actin-nucleating activity to endocytosis. The K994A mutant experiment (C39) demonstrates functional requirement, while the F-actin measurements (C40-C41) using both phalloidin and genome-edited neurons provide robust quantification.

results.result: Pharmacological stabilization of F-actin with jasplakinolide fully rescues both the endocytic kinetics and F-actin levels in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, demonstrating that reduced F-actin is the primary cause of the endocytic defect.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 provide strong rescue evidence with quantitative F-actin measurements showing restoration to control levels. This establishes causality between F-actin reduction and endocytic impairment, supporting the conclusion (C44).

results.result: RhoA is localized to the presynaptic compartment, and interference with Rho function delays synaptic vesicle endocytosis. mDia1/3 depletion reduces RhoA activity, consistent with a positive feedback loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 establish RhoA localization and function in endocytosis using both dominant-negative and knockdown approaches. The RhoA-GTP pulldown assay (C48) provides biochemical evidence for the feedback relationship with mDia1/3.

results.result: Rac1 activity is significantly elevated in mDia1/3-depleted neurons and upon RhoA/B inhibition, and Rac1 is equally distributed between pre- and postsynaptic compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 demonstrate compensatory Rac1 hyperactivation using Rac1-GTP pulldown assays under multiple conditions. The STED localization (C51) provides spatial context for Rac1 function.

results.result: Rac1 inhibition reduces presynaptic actin and delays endocytosis, while constitutively active Rac1 rescues endocytosis in mDia1/3-depleted neurons. Dominant-negative Rac1 exacerbates the mDia1/3 depletion phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 demonstrate Rac1's role through loss-of-function (C52-C54), gain-of-function (C55), and dominant-negative (C56) approaches. The lack of exocytic effects (C57) parallels other findings. However, C54 notes statistical limitations that slightly weaken the synergistic effect claim.

results.result: Perturbation of Cdc42 does not significantly affect synaptic vesicle endocytosis kinetics in control or mDia1/3-depleted neurons, indicating specificity for Rho and Rac1 pathways.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 provides important negative control data demonstrating pathway specificity. The lack of Cdc42 involvement distinguishes the Rho/Rac1 axis from other Rho family GTPases.

results.result: mDia1/3 depletion causes accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations and endosome-like vacuoles at synapses, with similar phenotypes observed in mDia1 knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide ultrastructural evidence for stalled endocytic intermediates using electron microscopy. The consistency between knockdown and knockout approaches (C61-C62) validates the findings.

results.result: Rac1 inhibition causes accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations but not endosome-like vacuoles. Combined mDia1/3 depletion and Rac1 inhibition synergistically increases invaginations, with similar morphological characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 demonstrate distinct ultrastructural phenotypes for Rac1 versus mDia1/3 perturbation. The synergistic effect on invaginations (C65) with similar morphology (C67) supports cooperative pathway function, though the ELV effect is not significant (C66).

results.result: mDia1/3-Rho and Rac1 signaling pathways cooperatively facilitate presynaptic endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling through interdependent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is a summary conclusion supported by the collective evidence from multiple experimental approaches showing biochemical interactions, functional interdependence, and synergistic phenotypes.

results.result: Loss of mDia1/3 causes delayed endocytosis without affecting exocytosis, accompanied by accumulation of membrane invaginations, vacuolar structures, and activity-dependent reduction in synaptic vesicle pool size.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 provide comprehensive summary of the mDia1/3 loss-of-function phenotype integrating functional and structural data from multiple figures.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence demonstrate that presynaptic actin facilitates endocytosis downstream of mDia/RhoA and Rac1 signaling: reduced F-actin in mDia1/3-depleted synapses, failure of actin polymerization-defective mDia1 to rescue, rescue by F-actin stabilization or constitutively active Rac1, and accumulation of mDia1 and F-actin at stalled endocytic sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 synthesize multiple experimental approaches providing converging mechanistic evidence. The combination of loss-of-function, structure-function, rescue, and localization data strongly supports the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The endocytic phenotype from mDia1/3 loss is milder than complete β- or γ-actin loss, likely due to partially redundant pathways for F-actin assembly. Unlike actin knockout neurons, mDia-depleted neurons do not show strong exocytic depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 provide important comparative context with prior literature. The inference about redundant pathways (C78) is reasonable given the Rac1 compensation data, and the lack of exocytic depression (C79) is documented with appropriate caveats.

results.result: Genetic loss of mDia1/3 partially phenocopies acute formin inhibition regarding membrane invaginations but additionally shows elevated endosome-like vacuoles, suggesting mDia may have additional roles in synaptic vesicle reformation downstream of endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 compare chronic genetic and acute pharmacological perturbations, identifying both similarities and differences. The inference about SV reformation (C82) is appropriately tentative and supported by citations.

results.result: The identified function of mDia1/3 in presynaptic endocytosis is consistent with actin-binding properties of endocytic proteins. The small size of accumulated invaginations argues against actomyosin-based constriction, favoring instead a model where F-actin couples exocytic membrane compression to endocytic pit formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 present mechanistic interpretations. While C83 is well-supported by literature, C84-C86 involve speculative mechanistic models. The size argument (C84) is reasonable but indirect, and the proposed F-actin ring model (C85-C86) relies heavily on a single citation (Ogunmowo et al., 2023) and ultrastructural observations that are consistent with but do not prove the model.

results.result: mDia1 controls presynaptic membrane contractility, potentially via recently identified presynaptic actin corrals in hippocampal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Deguchi et al., 2016; Bingham et al., 2023) that provide independent evidence for these phenomena.

results.result: Presynaptic endocytosis is regulated by interdependent yet partially redundant signaling for F-actin assembly downstream of Rho and Rac1, which control linear and branched F-actin networks that co-exist in presynaptic boutons.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 synthesize the major findings with appropriate citations. The interdependence is demonstrated experimentally, and the pathway functions (C90-C91) are well-established in the literature.

results.result: Loss of mDia1/3 or inhibition of Rho causes Rac1 hyperactivation, and dual loss of mDia1/3 and Rac1 function results in synergistic inhibitory effects on presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are directly supported by biochemical assays (Figures 5-7) showing Rac1 hyperactivation and synergistic functional/structural phenotypes with combined perturbations.

results.result: The signaling network regulating presynaptic actin assembly may have been evolutionarily selected for plasticity and resilience, potentially explaining contradictory results from drug-based manipulations in different models.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are speculative evolutionary interpretations. While the redundancy and compensation are well-documented experimentally, the evolutionary selection argument (C95) and explanation for literature discrepancies (C96) are plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Different actin pools may be differentially amenable to drug treatments due to tropomyosin association or variations in F-actin versus monomeric actin ratios, potentially explaining previously discrepant results.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are supported by appropriate citations (Bleckert et al., 2012; Gormal et al., 2017; Higashida et al., 2008) and provide reasonable explanations for literature inconsistencies.

results.result: Presynaptic actin assembly via mDia/Rho and Rac1 is predicted to facilitate all forms of presynaptic endocytosis operating on millisecond to second timescales at many synapse types, though further studies are needed.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is explicitly presented as a prediction requiring future testing. While supported by citations and the current data, it extends beyond what has been directly demonstrated.

results.result: Fast endophilin-mediated endocytosis (FEME) has been shown to be differentially regulated by actin and Rho GTPase family members.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is a factual statement about prior work supported by appropriate citations (Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017; Boucrot et al., 2015; Renard et al., 2015).

results.result: It is currently not understood how RhoA/B and Rac1 GTPase activation is integrated into the synaptic vesicle cycle or whether these GTPases operate at the same or different nanoscale sites and membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 appropriately acknowledge limitations and gaps in current understanding, identifying important questions for future research.

results.result: Pharmacological perturbation of actin dynamics using a cocktail of latrunculin A, jasplakinolide, and Y-27632 significantly slowed endocytic retrieval of both exogenously expressed Syph-pHluorin and endogenous vGAT without affecting exocytosis, demonstrating that a dynamic actin cytoskeleton facilitates presynaptic endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'successfully show that presynaptic membrane-associated actin is required for normal SV endocytosis' and notes the work uses 'state-of-the-art optical recording' with 'well-executed genetic and pharmacological perturbations.' No concerns are raised about these pharmacological experiments or their interpretation.

results.result: Genetic depletion of mDia1 alone or in combination with mDia3 significantly delayed SV endocytosis across multiple stimulation protocols and SV markers (Syph-pHluorin, vGLUT1-pHluorin, endogenous vGAT) without affecting exocytic fusion, with rescue experiments confirming specificity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these genetic manipulation findings. Reviewer 1 notes the authors use 'genetic modification of the amount of mDia1/3 by knock-down and knockout' to 'document the quantitative importance of each agent.' Reviewer 2 highlights 'further mechanistic insight regarding the specific function of mDia1/3' as a major strength. No concerns are raised about these core genetic experiments.

results.result: Application of IMM-01, a small molecule activator of mDia-related formins that relieves autoinhibition, led to moderate but significant acceleration of SV endocytosis without changing apparent SV fusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without critique. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'successfully show...that the rate of endocytosis is increased by activation of mDia1/3,' which directly references these IMM-01 experiments. The complementary gain-of-function approach strengthens the overall conclusion about mDia function.

results.result: Ultrastructural analysis by electron microscopy revealed reduced SV density in mDia1/3-depleted neurons and mDia1 knockout mice, with the phenotype rescued by silencing neuronal network activity with TTX.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly affirms that 'the analysis is augmented by ultrastructural analyses that demonstrate the quantitative changes in numbers of synaptic vesicles and in uncoated membrane invaginations that are predicted by the optical recordings.' This indicates acceptance of the EM findings including the SV density reduction and TTX rescue.

results.result: Mutant mDia1 lacking its N-terminal membrane-binding region (mDia1-ΔN) showed reduced membrane association and failed to rescue endocytosis defects, suggesting mDia acts by promoting actin assembly specifically at presynaptic membranes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'show that removal of the short amino-terminal portion of mDia1 that associates with the membrane interrupts the association of mDia1 with membrane actin in the presynaptic terminal,' directly affirming these structure-function experiments. The mechanistic interpretation is accepted without challenge.

results.result: Multicolor time-gated STED microscopy revealed that endogenous mDia1 is primarily localized to the presynaptic compartment, concentrated at or very close to (<50 nm) the plasma membrane.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the use of 'state-of-the-art' methods (Reviewer 1, 2) without questioning the STED localization data. The super-resolution imaging provides critical spatial information supporting the membrane-proximal function of mDia1, and no concerns are raised about these findings.

results.result: Quantitative proteomic analysis of mDia1 immunoprecipitates identified interaction partners including actin, Myosin IIB (concentrated at presynaptic membranes like mDia1), Rac1, and multiple endocytic proteins (Synaptojanin1, Amphiphysin, Endophilin A1, PACSIN1/2, Dynamin1).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these proteomic findings without critique. Reviewer 2 specifically highlights the work's contribution to understanding 'the control of both presynaptic actin dynamics and synaptic vesicle endocytosis,' which encompasses these molecular interaction data. The identification of endocytic protein interactions supports the mechanistic model.

results.result: Inhibition of dynamin (by Dynasore or dominant-negative Dynamin1 K44A) led to significant accumulation of mDia1 at presynaptic sites without affecting levels or distribution of synaptic markers Bassoon or Homer1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these findings. The accumulation of mDia1 upon dynamin inhibition provides evidence for mDia1's involvement in the endocytic process, and the specificity controls (no effect on Bassoon/Homer1) strengthen the interpretation. No methodological concerns are raised.

results.result: STED imaging showed presynaptic F-actin (labeled by phalloidin) in boutons marked by Bassoon, with levels significantly elevated upon dynamin inhibition (Dynasore treatment or Dynamin1 K44A expression).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the F-actin visualization and quantification without critique. Reviewer 1 notes the 'state-of-the-art optical recording' methods used throughout. The F-actin accumulation upon blocking endocytosis supports the model that actin dynamics are coupled to the endocytic process.

results.result: Actin polymerization-defective mDia1 mutant (K994A) failed to rescue endocytosis defects, and loss of mDia1/3 significantly reduced presynaptic F-actin levels (measured by phalloidin staining and in genome-engineered eGFP-Actb neurons).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the authors demonstrate that 'actin polymerization-defective mutant mDia1 (K994A) failed to restore delayed vGLUT1-pHluorin endocytosis,' directly affirming these critical structure-function experiments. The reduction in F-actin upon mDia1/3 loss provides direct mechanistic evidence for mDia's role in actin assembly.

results.result: Jasplakinolide treatment (F-actin stabilization) fully restored both endocytosis kinetics and presynaptic F-actin levels in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, leading to the conclusion that mDia1/3 facilitates SV endocytosis by regulating presynaptic F-actin.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this rescue experiment and conclusion without challenge. The jasplakinolide rescue is a key piece of evidence linking mDia function to actin regulation and endocytosis. Reviewer 1 notes the 'well-executed' experimental design, and no concerns are raised about this critical mechanistic conclusion.

results.result: STED imaging showed RhoA is primarily presynaptic, and interference with Rho function (dominant-negative RhoA/B or shRNA depletion) delayed SV endocytosis without affecting exocytosis; RhoA activity was reduced in mDia1/3-depleted neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these findings. Reviewer 2 states 'the major strength of the work was to reveal new information regarding the control of both presynaptic actin dynamics and synaptic vesicle endocytosis via Rho/Rac cascades,' directly affirming the Rho signaling results. The RhoA activity measurements provide biochemical support for the genetic/pharmacological findings.

results.result: Rac1 activity was significantly elevated in mDia1/3-depleted neurons and upon RhoA/B inhibition, consistent with antagonistic regulation of RhoA and Rac1; STED imaging showed Rac1 equally distributed between pre- and postsynaptic compartments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the Rho/Rac signaling network. Reviewer 2 highlights the 'significant advance in knowledge, with particular respect to Rho/Rac signalling' as a major strength. The reciprocal regulation of RhoA and Rac1 is a key mechanistic insight that reviewers do not question.

results.result: Pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 reduced presynaptic actin levels and delayed endocytic retrieval of endogenous vGAT, with a trend toward further aggravating the phenotype in mDia1/3-depleted neurons (though not statistically significant).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the Rac1 inhibition findings without critique. The observation that the additive effect did not reach significance is honestly reported and does not undermine the overall conclusion about Rac1's role. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'document the quantitative importance of each agent, and their synergistic relationship in regulation of endocytosis.'

results.result: Constitutively active Rac1 (Rac1-CA) rescued endocytosis in mDia1/3-depleted neurons, while dominant-negative Rac1 (Rac1-DN) delayed endocytosis and exacerbated the mDia1/3 loss phenotype; neither affected exocytosis. Perturbation of Cdc42 had no significant effect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these genetic rescue/perturbation experiments. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'show that RhoA activity and Rac1 activity act in a partially redundant and synergistic fashion together with mDia1/3 to regulate the rate of SV endocytosis.' The Rac1 rescue is critical evidence for the compensatory mechanism, and the Cdc42 negative result provides specificity.

results.result: Electron microscopy revealed accumulation of non-coated plasma membrane invaginations and elevated numbers of endosome-like vacuoles (ELVs) in mDia1/3-depleted neurons and mDia1 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly affirms that 'the analysis is augmented by ultrastructural analyses that demonstrate the quantitative changes in numbers of synaptic vesicles and in uncoated membrane invaginations that are predicted by the optical recordings.' This directly supports the EM findings of membrane invaginations and ELVs.

results.result: Rac1 inhibition led to accumulation of plasma membrane invaginations but not ELVs; combined mDia1/3 depletion and Rac1 blockade synergistically increased invaginations but not ELVs; both perturbations showed similar effects on invagination dimensions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these ultrastructural findings showing synergistic effects. Reviewer 1 notes the authors demonstrate 'synergistic inhibitory effects with respect to presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects,' directly affirming these EM results. The differential effects on invaginations vs. ELVs provide mechanistic insight into the stage of endocytosis affected.

results.result: The collective findings demonstrate that interdependent mDia1/3-Rho and Rac1 signaling pathways cooperatively act to facilitate presynaptic endocytosis and SV recycling.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is explicitly supported by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 states the work 'adds substantially to our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of SV endocytosis.' Reviewer 2 highlights 'significant advance in knowledge, with particular respect to Rho/Rac signalling' and notes 'further mechanistic insight regarding the specific function of mDia1/3.' The editor states the manuscript provides 'convincing evidence for the involvement of membrane actin, and its regulatory proteins, mDia1/3, RhoA, and Rac1 in the mechanism of synaptic vesicle re-uptake.'

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence support that presynaptic actin facilitates SV endocytosis downstream of mDia/RhoA and Rac1 signaling: (i) reduced presynaptic F-actin in mDia1/3-depleted synapses, (ii) failure of polymerization-defective mDia1 to rescue endocytosis, (iii) jasplakinolide rescue, (iv) constitutively-active Rac1 rescue, and (v) accumulation of mDia1 and F-actin under impaired dynamin-dependent endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this integrated mechanistic model. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'successfully show that presynaptic membrane-associated actin is required for normal SV endocytosis in the presynaptic terminal' and notes the work uses 'a wide variety of controlled perturbations' to establish the mechanism. All reviewers emphasize the mechanistic advance as a major strength.

results.result: The endocytic phenotype from mDia1/3 loss is milder than complete β- or γ-actin loss, likely reflecting partially redundant pathways for F-actin assembly at synapses; unlike actin KO neurons, mDia-depleted neurons did not show strong exocytic depression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparative analysis and interpretation without challenge. The acknowledgment of milder phenotypes and redundancy is consistent with the demonstrated compensatory mechanisms (e.g., Rac1 hyperactivation). No concerns are raised about these comparisons or the inference of pathway redundancy.

results.result: Genetic mDia1/3 loss partially phenocopies acute formin inhibition regarding membrane invaginations but, unlike acute inhibition, also shows elevated endosome-like vacuoles, suggesting an additional role for mDia in SV reformation downstream of endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question this comparison with prior acute inhibition studies or the inference about SV reformation. The distinction between acute and chronic perturbation effects is appropriately noted, and the speculation about additional roles is presented as a suggestion supported by the correlation with reduced SV numbers.

results.result: The identified function of mDia1/3-mediated actin assembly is consistent with actin-binding properties of endocytic proteins; the small size of accumulated invaginations renders actomyosin-based constriction unlikely, favoring instead a model where F-actin couples exocytic membrane compression to endocytic pit formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this mechanistic interpretation without challenge. The model is presented as a favored hypothesis supported by the ultrastructural observations and is consistent with recent literature cited. No concerns are raised about this interpretation or the dismissal of the constriction mechanism based on invagination size.

results.result: The findings are consistent with mDia1 controlling presynaptic membrane contractility and recently identified presynaptic actin corrals; presynaptic endocytosis is regulated by interdependent yet partially redundant signaling for F-actin assembly downstream of Rho (linear networks) and Rac1 (branched networks) that co-exist in presynaptic boutons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this integrated model. Reviewer 2 states 'the major strength of the work was to reveal new information regarding the control of both presynaptic actin dynamics and synaptic vesicle endocytosis via Rho/Rac cascades.' The connection to linear vs. branched actin networks and the redundancy/interdependence of pathways is a key conceptual advance that reviewers affirm.

results.result: Loss of mDia1/3 or Rho inhibition causes Rac1 hyperactivation, and dual loss of mDia1/3 and Rac1 function results in synergistic inhibitory effects on presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'show that RhoA activity and Rac1 activity act in a partially redundant and synergistic fashion together with mDia1/3 to regulate the rate of SV endocytosis' and demonstrate 'synergistic inhibitory effects with respect to presynaptic endocytosis and ultrastructural defects.' This is identified as a major mechanistic advance.

results.result: The signaling network regulating presynaptic actin assembly may have been evolutionarily selected for plasticity and resilience, potentially explaining contradictory results from drug-based manipulations in past studies; different actin pools may be differentially amenable to drug treatments due to tropomyosin association or F-actin/G-actin ratios.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these speculative interpretations, which are appropriately presented as possible explanations for literature discrepancies. The discussion of network resilience and drug resistance mechanisms is supported by citations and helps contextualize the findings within the broader literature. No concerns are raised about these interpretations.

results.result: The authors predict that presynaptic actin assembly via mDia/Rho and Rac1 facilitates all forms of presynaptic endocytosis operating on millisecond-to-second timescales and at many synapse types; fast endophilin-mediated endocytosis (FEME) shows similar differential regulation by actin and Rho GTPases.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this prediction as appropriately speculative and supported by the data. The comparison to FEME is noted without challenge. The authors appropriately acknowledge that 'further studies will be needed to test this hypothesis,' and reviewers do not object to this forward-looking statement.

results.result: It is not currently understood if/how RhoA/B and Rac1 GTPase activation is nested into the SV cycle or whether these GTPases operate at the same or different nanoscale sites and membranes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this acknowledgment of current limitations without critique. The honest statement of what remains unknown is appropriate and does not detract from the substantial mechanistic advances demonstrated. No reviewer suggests this gap undermines the conclusions.
